papers.title: PsyBer-Agent: A Psychology-Driven User Agent for Recommender Systems
papers.abstract: Evaluating recommender systems before deployment requires simulators that remain realistic over long, closed-loop interaction cycles. Current LLM-based agents generally function as surface imitators that generate realistic short-term responses but fail to capture the underlying user dynamics such as fatigue, affect, and shifting preferences. We propose PsyBer-Agent, a psychology-inspired simulator that models these dynamics through its Psy-Engine. This engine represents each user with three evolving, model-defined latent states. To calibrate simulated behavior against real interaction logs, we align log-conditioned reference trajectories with simulator-generated latent-state trajectories via Unbalanced Gromov--Wasserstein optimal transport. This approach provides structured supervision for a lightweight policy without the computational burden of fine-tuning the backbone LLM. We also introduce WebSim and the PsyBer Benchmark, which encompass multimodal scenarios and seven recommender backbones. Our framework evaluates behavioral fidelity, latent-state consistency, robustness, and responses to social-cue perturbations. On the tested horizons, PsyBer-Agent shows lower behavioral discrepancy than the prompt-only simulators while maintaining stable performance under large-scale concurrent simulation for up to 5M queued simulation tasks under bounded concurrency. Code is available in the supplementary material and at: PsyBer-Agent: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CC66F/, WebSim Platform: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/D8EAX/.

papers.title: Artificiality's First Exam: An LLM-Referenced C-test for Supraintelligence
papers.abstract: Under the accelerated pace of AI development, any benchmark whose difficulty is calibrated with humans or current AI systems becomes circular, or saturates soon. How can we then evaluate machines that may become more capable than the current machines and the people who write the tests? One answer to the question hinges on inverse problems, inductive inference questions for which difficulty depends on the complexity of the underlying mechanism, given the observations and the previous knowledge. Levin's Kt, a computable variant of Kolmogorov complexity, puts a theoretical upper bound to that difficulty, balancing the simplest representation encoding for the mechanism and the logarithm of the time steps to run that mechanism. Previous tests derived from Levin's Kt, such as the original C-test, are based on minimalistic Universal Turing Machines (UTM), capable of very limited representations and no previous knowledge. Reasoning large language models (LLM) are UTMs that capture a compendium of human culture as knowledge, using prompts as natural language programs. This paper presents the first test based on Levin's Kt with LLMs as representational machines. Fresh test items can be produced at high difficulties, estimated in a ratio scale measured in bits, before any human or frontier model can solve them. We formalise the measure, devise a lightweight generation and certification pipeline, explore the effect of the power of the reference machine and the gap between examiner and examinee. We produce a first battery of certified items administered to twelve LLMs. The resulting agent characteristic curves decrease with difficulty, down to the uncharted high-difficulty region, the supra-intelligence window of items we can certify, yet beyond generations of frontier intelligence.

papers.title: Loose Lips: Understanding Privacy Leakage in Agentic Dialogue
papers.abstract: As LLM agents are increasingly deployed in high-stakes enterprise settings, understanding how they handle sensitive information in agentic dialogue has become critical. Privacy leakage in such settings requires reasoning about whether information flows respect the contextual norms under which they originated. We extend CIMemories to CIMEMORIES DIALOGUE, a benchmark of 4,410 two-agent dialogue instances grounded in Contextual Integrity theory. Using this benchmark, we systematically evaluate 7 open-weight models from the Qwen3 and Llama 3.1 families across conversation lengths of 1 and 6 turns under three prompting conditions. We find that task capability and privacy leakage are fundamentally coupled: more capable models are systematically leakier, with no model in our evaluation able to decouple the two. Thinking models consistently leak more than their non-thinking counterparts, a pattern we attribute to the extended reasoning surface created by chain-of-thought. Leakage compounds with conversation length, rising up to 3x from 1 to 6 turns. Our results suggest that the coupling between task capability and privacy leakage is not an artifact of misconfiguration but a structural feature of current agentic systems.

papers.title: Is the Future Predictable? Modeling Future Predictability for Reliable Temporal Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain unreliable when reasoning about the future. Existing models often overlook the difference among future states, committing to specific answers even when the queried facts are inherently volatile. To capture this challenge, we introduce ChronoRegime, a future-oriented temporal reasoning task that requires models to determine whether historical temporal evidence justifies commitment to a future answer. Furthermore, we propose Confidence-Aware Temporal Reasoning (CTR), a framework that estimates future predictability from temporal dynamics and regulates answer commitment accordingly. Rather than performing unconditional forecasting, CTR commits only when the reconstructed evidence supports the target future state. Across multiple LLMs, CTR improves strict overall accuracy by 6.7 percentage points and reduces hallucination rates by 18.4 percentage points on average over the plain QA baseline. These results demonstrate that explicit predictability assessment is an effective mechanism for safer and more reliable temporal reasoning under future uncertainty.

papers.title: Fin_Agent at FinEval 2026: Task-Aware Methods for Multilingual Financial NLP
papers.abstract: We present Fin_Agent, our submission to the FinEval 2026 shared task on multilingual fi nancial language understanding. Our sys tems address Greek financial named-entity recognition, Japanese implicit communication recognition, and multilingual financial ques tion answering. For Greek NER, we com bine annotation-aware numeric rules with zero shot Qwen2.5-32B classification, achieving 0.9521 public F1 and 0.8884 private F1. For Japanese implicit communication, an inter pretable cue-based ordinal scorer achieves 98.0% test accuracy. For multilingual financial QA, BGE-M3retrieval with Qwen3-32B gen eration achieves 0.3023 and 0.3419 ROUGE-1 F1 on the public and private splits. Key limita tions include dataset-specific rules, handcrafted cues, and limited supervision. Implementa tion code is available https://github.com/ Rashidnira/finagent-fineval-2026.

papers.title: Does System One Transfer? Calibrated Typed-Decision Models, Label Budgets, and Translation for Indonesian Regional Languages
papers.abstract: Calibrated typed-decision ("System One") models return a label and a probability in a single forward pass at a small fraction of the cost of large language models (LLMs), yet their evaluation has been almost entirely English. We report a pre-registered evaluation of the commercial Jev model and the open Laya-multilingual model on Indonesian regional languages, using the parallel NusaX sentiment (12 languages) and NusaTranslation sentiment and emotion (7 languages) test sets. Jev is more often correct on sentences that are lexically closer to Indonesian in all three datasets, and presenting the human Indonesian translation instead raises its accuracy by up to 37.2 points, most in languages distant from Indonesian. Its expected calibration error does not grow on regional languages, but its ability to rank its own errors degrades in all three datasets. Retrained classifiers need more than 500 labels per language to match zero-shot Jev in 9 of 10 NusaX regional languages. A confidence-gated cascade that sends Jev's 10-30% least confident decisions to a local IndoBERT classifier matches or exceeds the better of the two systems, and routing to an LLM instead matches that LLM at 24-77% lower API cost. Of six further commercial LLMs (three Claude and three GPT models), five are 4-14 points more accurate than Jev, at several hundred times the API cost where it is reported, while the smallest (Claude Haiku) is less accurate. We release the pre-registration, code and all predictions.

papers.title: ClawLoop: Self-Improving Agents via Harness-Native Training Loop
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven their deployment toward general-purpose harness environments, where LLM-based agents operate in sandbox workspaces and interact directly with file systems and shells. While numerous post-training pipelines exist for tool-use agents, their counterparts for harness-based agents remain scarce and are predominantly one-shot and teacher-dependent: a stronger external model synthesizes tasks and collects trajectories, the target agent is trained once, and evaluation results are consumed by human researchers rather than fed back into the loop. Such pipelines are inherently bounded by the capability of the external model and the scope of human prior, leaving no room for self-improvement. To address these limitations, we propose ClawLoop, a framework that enables self-improving without any external teacher model and with minimal prior dependencies. ClawLoop composes three phases into a self-sustaining cycle: Task Synthesis, which generates a diverse pool of training tasks via two complementary construction routines, applies diagnosis-conditioned difficulty growth followed by both agent-free and agent-based task validation; Training, which updates the agent via SFT and/or RL; and Diagnosis and Feedback, which analyzes the agent's rollout behaviors to produce a capability analysis report that will be used as feedback for task synthesis in the next iteration. Using Qwen3.6-27B as the loop model, ClawLoop yields consistent improvements on SkillsBench, Claw-Eval-Live, and ClawGym-Bench. The iteratively refined tasks are further transferred to smaller-scale Qwen3.5-4B and 9B models with gains across all benchmarks, validating data quality independently of the loop model.

papers.title: Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallel sampling for faster generation than autoregressive models, an increasingly important advantage as inference becomes a dominant computational workload. However, DLMs degrade quickly with fewer sampling steps, process the full sequence at every step, and require many passes over the dataset to reach good quality. We introduce Next-Concept Modeling (NCM), a two-stage, coarse-to-fine framework: a multiscale residual VQ-VAE encodes text into a hierarchy of discrete codes, and a transformer generates one level at a time, predicting all codes within a level in parallel. At matched parameter scales, NCM achieves better generative perplexity than the strongest DLM baseline on LM1B while running $21\times$ faster. On OpenWebText, NCM is competitive with the strongest DLM while running $10\times$ faster; on XSum, it matches the strongest DLM's ROUGE-L while being $31\times$ faster. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations.

papers.title: Unconstrained CTI-REALM with Open-Weights
papers.abstract: Organisations that want language-model agents for security work face a choice between open-weight models, which they can run and audit themselves, and far more expensive closed frontier models. We study that choice on CTI-REALM (arXiv:2603.13517), a benchmark in which an agent turns a threat-intelligence report into a working detection by querying a live telemetry store. We evaluate twenty-six models, nineteen open-weight and seven closed, under a common harness, scorer and panel of LLM judges. Our main finding is that an open-weight model can match the strongest closed models at less than a tenth of their cost, provided it is given enough turns. The benchmark's published limit on agent messages is a confound: a task that exhausts the limit scores zero on every checkpoint, including those it had already passed, so results at that limit partly measure which models finish in time. At the published limit the leading open-weight and closed models cannot be distinguished. With the limit relaxed, the models it was truncating recover, and the highest rewards belong to open-weight models. Among the leading models, price is a poor guide to capability: models with similar rewards differ in cost by more than an order of magnitude. Because the benchmark's checkpoint scores largely record what an agent did or mentioned, we also introduce stage-level metrics that score what the agent submits, by executing its detection queries in the telemetry store and judging its outputs against the answer key. Rather than combining them into one more overall reward, we show that different models lead different stages, which suggests routing each stage of the workflow to the model that performs it best rather than choosing a single model by its overall score. We also report how many tokens each model generates, and find that the share of output spent on thinking does not track the reward.

papers.title: Modeling the Arrival Time of Information-Bearing Events in Natural Language
papers.abstract: Understanding how information is distributed over time is fundamental to modeling natural language. While existing empirical studies primarily rely on post-hoc analysis of information-theoretic metrics, such as surprisal, little is known about the generation processes under the surface. We propose a novel approach for addressing this gap using the tool of neural temporal point processes (TPPs) by modeling the key information-bearing events in text sequences with learnable event intensity functions. Our model takes the history of event intervals and the contextual semantic representations from LLMs as input, and predicts the future arrival times for two types of events: new-word and high-surprisal-token. The experimental results reveal an interesting distinction in event intensities: LLMs tend to produce new words at significantly higher rates than humans, while high-surprisal tokens do not exhibit the difference. A decaying pattern of intensity over time is found in new-word events for both humans and LLMs, but not in high-surprisal-token events. Our findings revisit and extend previous studies that use simpler methods; provide supplementary evidence for theories about constrained context representation inherent in human language production; and find a new angle to view human and LLM generation differences.

papers.title: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World
papers.abstract: LLM agents' capabilities depend not only on their underlying models but also on their execution harnesses. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a promising approach to automatically evolve these harnesses. However, deploying RSI in open-world settings still faces two critical challenges. First, open-world tasks are typically unseen during the harness design phase and novel at test time, leaving no ground-truth verifiers to reliably guide online harness edits. Second, the RSI process remains highly task-specific and fails to generalize to novel scenarios. We introduce Harness^2, a plug-and-play, recursive agent harnessing framework that addresses these challenges through two connected levels of recursion. Task-level recursion refines the current task's harness using a contrastive Propose-Probe-Compose step that reliably guides edits without ground-truth verifiers, and can be scaled further via parallel or sequential recursion. Harnessing-level recursion then extracts experience from these edits to update a continual improvement harness, enabling the agent to better adapt to future tasks. Across three professional benchmarks and four model-harness configurations, a single step consistently improves GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash over their base harnesses, yielding gains of up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 points on JobBench, and 11.8 percentage points on LAB, with further gains as the task-level recursion budget increases.

papers.title: Agentic Data Engineering for LLMs: System Design and a Controlled Empirical Study
papers.abstract: LLM data engineering requires iterative experimentation to determine how data selection, rewards, and curricula affect model learning, making it a natural setting for AI-for-AI (AI4AI) research. Can agents use experimental feedback to progressively improve strategies, and do the resulting strategies improve target-model performance on held-out data? We study how agents use experimental feedback to develop data-engineering strategies under fixed training and evaluation protocols. Our Agentic Data Engineering (ADE) framework lets agents pursue, revise, or combine research directions using cumulative findings. Strategies are selected by in-loop scores and evaluated on held-out benchmarks. Across four tasks-math and code data selection, math reward design, and math curriculum learning-selected strategies achieve absolute gains over generic baselines of up to 13.34% on AIME25 Pass@32 and 5.85% averaged across four held-out benchmarks under fixed training conditions. In-loop scores improve over successive experiments, while held-out trajectories show that later in-loop gains do not always improve generalization. Comparisons of research organization and feedback access favor combining evidence analysis with cumulative findings. Research trajectories show how earlier findings inform strategy revisions and combinations across research directions.

papers.title: The Thinking Leakage in Reinforcement Learning for LLMs
papers.abstract: Hybrid reasoning models such as the Qwen3 series switch between a THINK mode and a NO-THINK mode through a few chat-template tokens. A popular recipe trains such models with reinforcement learning in NO-THINK mode and reports improved reasoning performance. We provide evidence that much of this gain can be explained by thinking leakage: the gain comes largely from partially reactivating the reasoning abilities of the original model's THINK mode instead of learning enhanced reasoning behavior. We train Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B with GRPO in NO-THINK mode. As accuracy improves, responses become longer and more reflective, are increasingly judged by the original model to resemble its own thinking, and the model's internal activations shift toward its THINK mode. We then investigate at the level of weights, activations, and attention heads: scaling the RL update further elicits THINK-mode behavior and approaches THINK-mode accuracy but does not exceed it; in Qwen3-8B, replacing a low-dimensional THINK-related activation subspace of the RL-trained model with its original-model value removes most of the RL gain, and the reverse exchange transfers a considerable fraction of the gain to the original model; and the RL-induced shift passes through the attention heads that read the empty think block. We further identify a possible mechanism in the GRPO training signal: responses favored by the advantage-weighted update are more THINK-like, and a gradient step computed from this signal moves the model toward its THINK state. Thus, gains in NO-THINK mode can largely reflect reactivation of reasoning abilities already present in the original model.

papers.title: ASSET: Adaptive Speech Segmentation via Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Speech large language models (LLMs) are often built using pretrained acoustic encoders as an audio interface to an LLM decoder. However, LLMs scale poorly with input sequence length, while acoustic encoders tend to produce substantially longer sequences than typical textual inputs. This motivates learning to compress encoder outputs while preserving task-oriented information. To this end, we introduce ASSET, a reinforcement learning (RL)-based framework that learns to adaptively compress encoder outputs by first partitioning them into variable-duration segments and then pooling each segment into a continuous audio token. We use group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) to train a segmenter with task performance feedback and a token-rate penalty. In automatic speech recognition (ASR) experiments, ASSET achieves performance comparable to a transcript-assisted character-boundary oracle with approximately 25% fewer audio tokens on English LibriSpeech, while improving on a phone-boundary oracle at a similar token rate on Mandarin AISHELL. Exploratory experiments on non-ASR tasks further illustrate how learned segmentation changes when the framework is adapted to tasks beyond transcription.

papers.title: Which Metadata Matters for LLM Tool Selection in MCP? Evidence from Controlled Factor-Level Interventions
papers.abstract: In Model Context Protocol (MCP) systems, LLMs select tools from metadata rather than from their implementations. Names and descriptions summarize what a tool does, while the parameter schema specifies the fields a tool accepts and how they are organized. Our analysis of metadata for 367,174 MCP tools reveals substantial schema variation among functionally similar tools. Many of these tools share names and similar descriptions but expose different parameter schemas. This raises a key question: can parameter-schema differences influence tool selection before any call is made? We study this question through controlled metadata interventions across five LLMs and five tasks. Each comparison changes exactly one metadata factor (server name, tool name, description, or parameter schema) while keeping the others fixed. We balance tool positions and use conditional logistic regression to estimate position-adjusted effects. We find that: (1) parameter-schema changes produce the largest and most consistent selection shifts among the tested interventions. Models tend to favor separate top-level parameters over grouped or composite forms. (2) Descriptions that explain parameters also tend to increase selection, while name effects are weaker and less consistent. (3) Targeted comparisons show that schema effects depend on the specific parameter names and on how the request represents the same information. When only one schema satisfies an explicit request requirement, all five models select the compatible tool despite position preferences. These results show that parameter schemas influence not only how tools are called, but also whether they are selected. For MCP developers and evaluators, schema design and tool ordering can therefore affect which implementation is invoked even when functionality is unchanged.

papers.title: Evaluating LLMs as Agentic Workflow Executors in Real-World Customer Support Skills
papers.abstract: Enterprise customer-support agents increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) to execute bounded, tool-using workflows. We study this problem through the lens of Skill LLMs: specialized executors that operate within a selected skill context and must complete a narrow, stateful workflow under policy and tool constraints. We present a benchmark construction pipeline that mines recurrent workflows from real-world transcripts, converts them into structured skill descriptions, maps them to tool requirements, simulates environment state with Model Context Protocol (MCP)-compatible mocks, and generates multi-turn tool-using dialogues. Using this benchmark, we conduct a large-scale zero-shot evaluation of 17 language models spanning closed model families and deployment-oriented open-weight models from 1.7B to 14B parameters, each judged independently by five strong LLM judges, plus a deterministic rule-based evaluator that checks tool coverage, hallucinated tool use, and unsupported claims. We find a consistent ranking in which GPT-5.4 leads by a wide margin and QWEN3.5-9B is the strongest open-weight model (below 20B), outperforming several closed baselines under every judge. We also find that judge choice is not a negligible methodological detail: pairwise judge agreement on the pass/fail verdict averages Kappa=0.524 across 10 judge pairs. These results suggest that comprehensive zero-shot evaluation of skill execution requires judge reliability as carefully as model capability.

papers.title: Multimodal Co-Generation With Continuous Bitstream Diffusion
papers.abstract: We show that continuous bitstream diffusion (CoBit), originally developed for language modeling, provides a unified framework for joint and conditional multimodal generation using the same training and sampling protocol. Across image-text, speech-text and protein sequence-structure modeling, models are trained separately from scratch, but each uses a single input projection, transformer backbone, bitwise prediction head and binary score-matching objective shared across its modalities. Within each setting, a single checkpoint supports joint generation and the conditional directions included in training by changing which parts of the bitstream are observed. We first validate the approach on MNIST-Sum, a controlled image-text task pairing raw binary images with equations encoded as text, achieving near-perfect conditional accuracy and high joint consistency without learned tokenizers. We then apply the same protocol at larger scale to speech-text and protein sequence-structure modeling. Trained without text pretraining, a single speech-text model performs speech synthesis, recognition, continuation, and unconditional co-generation. Jointly generated speech and text achieve 3.5% word error rate between the generated text and automatic transcriptions of the generated speech. In protein modeling, a single CoBit checkpoint supports forward folding, inverse folding, and joint sequence-structure generation. For jointly generated proteins spanning 100-500 residues, computational refolding of CoBit's sequences yields structures that agree with the generated backbones at a mean self-consistency TM-score of 0.911. Together, these results show that CoBit provides a common generative framework for substantially different modalities and forms of cross-modal dependence, without introducing a domain-specific objective or sampling procedure.

papers.title: Tokenization-Invariant Watermarking: A Byte-Local Method for LLM Text
papers.abstract: We introduce Tokenization-Invariant Watermarking (TI-WM), a method that embeds a watermark during token generation but keys and scores it on canonicalized UTF-8 bytes. The detector does not invoke the tokenizer. Canonicalizer-preserving edits leave its score unchanged; other localized canonical-byte edits affect a bounded number of scoring windows. Across three fixed keys and 128 prompts per key and model, a deterministic white-box attack at a 5% word-edit budget leaves mean attacked-AUC 0.530 on Qwen3-8B and 0.664 on Gemma 4 E4B, compared with 0.410 and 0.489 for Unigram with detection-side deletion. These operating points are not jointly matched on quality and clean detectability. Bias sweeps show model-dependent distortion costs, and shared-rule controls support a locality interpretation without establishing a unique advantage of bytes. Visible insertion outside the canonicalizer's deletion set defeats the default design. Alphabetic filtering closes that channel but does not resolve source shift or calibrated detection power. TI-WM thus provides a concrete construction with local scoring guarantees and measured attack-ranking gains, not a general robustness or low-false-positive-rate deployment guarantee.

papers.title: SciCurateBench: Curating Experimental Data from Heterogeneous Scientific Literature with Verbal-Action Agents
papers.abstract: Scientific research increasingly depends on curating experimental data from literature. Scientific data curation requires verifying exact experimental conditions (e.g., specific assays, clinical outcomes, and data availability) across long, heterogeneous files, which is a highly time-consuming process. Existing benchmarks evaluate only broad relevance on short queries, failing to capture this complexity. We introduce SciCurateBench, a benchmark of 200 expert-annotated papers from major life-science journals that challenges systems to verify conjunctive biological experimental criteria from raw, unprocessed scientific literature. We show that plain LLMs and popular reasoning, tool-using, and feedback-based agents all struggle with this task. To study what makes the task tractable, we further propose LangPoli, an integrative system in which a policy agent generates natural language action guidelines that actor agents convert into executable tools. LangPoli showed strong performance on both Paper Classification (83.16% F1 vs. 58.22% for its base LLM) and Structured Information Retrieval, and also improves re-ranking on the public benchmarks of LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC. We further explore curriculum transfer, a method that distills generalizable strategies from solved tasks to accelerate the solving of related problems. We hope this work facilitates research in truly practical scientific AI assistance. The anonymized pre-release can be found from https://anonymous.4open. science/r/scicuratebench-D885/.

papers.title: RealityBench: Simulated Environments to Evaluate a Vision Language Model's Ability to Document Human Physical Work
papers.abstract: Augmenting worker capabilities in the physical world through guidance has been a decades-long goal for AI agents. One key supporting capability is to understand what the worker is doing, seeing through the human's camera or smart glasses, and assist them in documentation. Despite advances in vision language models, their capabilities in these settings remain uncertain and are challenging to benchmark because most physical work data is proprietary, and involves too much variability to study in a principled manner. Unlike structured settings such as kitchens and warehouses that have predictable lighting, geometry, and objects, field-facing tasks such as rooftop solar installation and vehicle repair are unconstrained and high variance. Here, we model real-world physical work in Blender across eleven environments, incorporating variants in both image acceptability and documentation. The acceptability task asks whether a particular view would be suitable proof-of-work and documentation asks whether an agent can understand the task-relevant state of the environment from that view. Across 26 vision-language models, we find that top models largely solve documentation when the answer is text in frame, but are weak at reading measurements and at judging small parts and spatial relations, such as whether a tape measure leans. Acceptability is harder to pin down because human raters disagree with each other. Measured against a scorer that agrees with the raters' majority about as often as a single rater does, the best models cannot be distinguished from a single non-author rater, at a cost within the range of a human pass. In the three environments where we can trace acceptability errors, most wrong rejections come from misreading the scene rather than the requirement. On the three documentation questions for which we have real images, model rankings on rendered frames transfer to real images.

papers.title: Scaling Laws for Multimodal Data Mixtures
papers.abstract: Frontier AI systems are increasingly natively multimodal, jointly pretrained on multiple modalities, such as text, vision, and audio. However, the scientific understanding of the multimodal data mixtures used to pretrain these systems --- how much of each modality to mix, and at what potential interference cost to the others --- is largely absent or gatekept. In this work, we derive data mixing scaling laws for three modalities: text, vision, and audio. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly adopt Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, as MoEs scale efficiently and partially limit cross-modal interference. We therefore use MoEs to conduct 268 experiments ranging from 457M to 8.3B parameters, on up to 150 billion tokens. Our work leads to multiple actionable insights into multimodal data mixing for training MLLMs. First, compute optima are modality-specific: audio modality is model-heavy, favoring scaling parameters over tokens, while text and vision require balanced scaling of model size and data. Second, repeating vision or audio data beyond 2x yields negligible benefits. Finally, cross-modal interactions are highly asymmetric: vision strongly interferes with audio, whereas audio's interference with learning text and vision is negligible. Overall, we provide a principled foundation for understanding the multimodal data mixtures needed to train frontier MLLMs.

papers.title: MemForm: Benchmarking Memory Formation Poisoning in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables LLM agents to learn from past interactions but exposes memory formation to adversarial influence. Existing studies primarily organize memory poisoning by attack channels, corruption patterns, or lifecycle stages, leaving formation interfaces insufficiently characterized. We formulate Memory Formation Poisoning as adversarial manipulation of the interfaces through which persistent agent memory is produced and committed, and introduce MemForm, a controlled diagnostic benchmark covering five interfaces: Content, Evidence, Scope, Selection, and Path Poisoning. We introduce Selection and Path Poisoning as controlled intervention categories that isolate retention and consolidation order effects, respectively. Each category pairs clean and poisoned conditions with interface-specific controls. Evaluations across six LLMs and two response formats reveal broad susceptibility at all five interfaces under the evaluated memory protocols and implementations. Crucially, authentic experiences with successful outcomes do not guarantee reliable behavior after memory formation: changes to contextual support, retention, or consolidation order can induce undesirable downstream behavior. In particular, consolidation order can alter behavior even with identical retained experiences, depending on the memory formation procedure. Additional analyses show that interface applicability depends on memory architecture and that Path Poisoning susceptibility depends on the updater. The evaluated defenses provide incomplete mitigation that varies by interface. These findings motivate protecting both what is committed to persistent memory and how memory is formed from experiences. Code and data are available at https://github.com/opanhw/memform-code.

papers.title: Neither True nor False: Do LLMs Represent Truth-Value Gaps in Plural Predication?
papers.abstract: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) genuinely grasp the truth conditions of plural descriptions, or do they force every sentence into true or false? We investigate the Homogeneity Gap, a semantic phenomenon where a plural definite (e.g., the kids laughed) and its negation (the kids didn't laugh) are both neither true nor false when only some of the kids laughed, whereas their quantified counterparts (all, not all) remain strictly bivalent. We introduce HomogeneityNLI, a diagnostic dataset of 1,000 minimal-pair items crossing determiner, polarity, and group composition across ten logical conditions. Evaluating seven open-weight models, we uncover a pervasive Bivalence Bias: models assign plural definites their homogeneous truth conditions, reading the kids as all of them and the kids didn't as none of them, yet collapse the truth-value gap into falsity. In the zero-shot setting, no model recognizes the gap for both polarities in more than 15% of scenarios, and negated definites are judged False in 84% of cases. Explicit linguistic rules, chain-of-thought, and enumeration prompts produce unstable, model-specific effects that often entrench the bias. Taken together, our findings indicate that current open-weight LLMs have acquired the truth conditions of plural predication but not its trivalent logic.

papers.title: Evaluating Semantic Relation Knowledge through Bidirectional Relation Prediction from Gloss Pairs
papers.abstract: Semantic relations organise word senses and are fundamental to lexical semantics. In order to evaluate semantic relation knowledge of large language models (LLMs), we propose a challenging task in which an LLM predicts the relation between two glosses (definitions of senses) presented in two different orders. The predictions for the two orders are evaluated for consistency with the symmetry or asymmetry of semantic relations. Our task is designed for both monolingual and cross-lingual evaluation, allowing us to examine whether relation knowledge remains accessible when the same senses are verbalised through glosses in different languages. We construct a dataset of 3,069 sense pairs, with each sense verbalised in English, Greek, Romanian, Turkish, and Japanese. Experiments with 17 LLMs in zero-shot and five-shot settings reveal generally poor performance. In each setting, only eight LLMs achieve a macro-averaged F1 score significantly above a random baseline, and only one (zero-shot) and two (five-shot) significantly outperform a neural baseline. In particular, LLMs often fail to generate bidirectionally consistent predictions for hypernymy and to make correct predictions for holonymy in either direction. Our results suggest limitations in current LLMs' semantic relation knowledge, both in identifying relations and in respecting asymmetry.

papers.title: Evaluating Bias in Chinese Large Language Models across Tasks and Registers: Task Operationalization Effects and Irony Classification Risks
papers.abstract: In Chinese content governance, large language models are increasingly used to identify toxic and discriminatory expressions, yet both task operationalization and ironic expression can alter bias measurement readings. We conducted a preregistered multi-task behavioral audit of multiple Chinese large language models. In the content classification experiment, the core panel's classification error rate rose from 10.9% in the formal register to 23.5% in the yinyang (an echoic-irony register) version, a risk difference of +12.7 percentage points. (95% CI [+9.7, +15.7]). Inter-rater agreement was lower in the yinyang register (majority-vote kappa = 0.299), so the increase contains a component of label uncertainty propagation, but the direction of increase was consistent under both adjudicated and majority-vote reference standards. Explicit irony-aware prompts reduced the intervention panel's error rate by 9.6 percentage points. We operationalized the 29 shared proposition anchors into three task forms: social consensus estimation (Form A), high-stakes decision (Form B), and controlled association rating (Form C); independent manipulation checks found that all 58 A-C comparison units received unanimous agreement, whereas the low A-B convergence was confirmed by calibrated majority adjudication (87.8% supporting the minority judgment); on the irony-probe materials, the interactions of B and C relative to A were +0.577 and +1.121, respectively. Thus, when evaluating large language models for Chinese content governance, the effect of task operationalization on bias readings is an empirical question that requires data to answer, and safety evaluation should incorporate the ironic register as a test condition.

papers.title: EdgeLLM-Nano: Auditing Polar-Guided Key-Cache Compression and Consistency-Anchored Pruning on a 33.6 MB On-Device Language Model
papers.abstract: Deploying language models (LMs) on the edge presents unique memory, latency, and power challenges absent in high-performance computing. KV-cache compression emerges as a promising approach to address these challenges. However, the effectiveness of current KV-cache compression methods has not been thoroughly examined on edge devices. Moreover, we show that existing evaluation methods do not always involve the KV-cache under test. We propose EdgeLLM-Nano, a measurement study of KV-cache compression using a nano-scale decoder-only LM (transformer) testbed that has 8.39M parameters, i.e., 33.6 MB, to enable end-to-end examination of each backend, seed, and power sample. Our results give a negative verdict for a polar-guided key-cache quantizer (round-to-nearest (RTN) control causes an order of magnitude less damage), as well as a consistency-anchored progressive weight pruner (one-shot magnitude-based pruning performs as well as, if not better). We also introduce Long-Context Decode Fidelity (LCDF) evaluation, a token-by-token examination of teacher-forced log-losses using the KV-cache under test. Unlike perplexity that gives the same 5.461 score to all methods, LCDF distinguishes different KV-cache compression backends thanks to its paired statistics across seeds and effect sizes. Our companion Raspberry Pi 5 measurement shows all compression backends we tested to be less energy-efficient per token compared to uncompressed FP16 inference. Except for KIVI that is close to lossless in terms of LCDF, our findings indicate KV-cache compression can be improved. LCDF offers a simple and effective way of shedding light on KV-cache compression methods, whose negative impacts have been overlooked by perplexity.

papers.title: Scale, Drivers, and Limits of Representational Alignment Across Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Comparing large language models can reveal shared representational structure and systematic differences between them. However, aggregate similarity measures can obscure how agreement varies across geometric scales and which linguistic properties support it. We introduce two complementary methods to resolve where models agree and what supports that agreement. Standard representational similarity analysis (RSA) summarizes similarity across all stimulus pairs, potentially obscuring differences in alignment between nearby and distant inputs. Neighborhood-Weighted RSA (NW-RSA) addresses this limitation by weighting stimulus pairs according to their proximity in representational space, placing alignment from local neighborhoods to global geometry on a common scale. Counterfactual RSA (CF-RSA) tests which linguistic properties support alignment by comparing intact representations in one model with representations under controlled linguistic perturbations in another. Across diverse language models, we find strong agreement in coarse representational geometry but substantial divergence in local neighborhoods. Alignment is observed both across broadly sampled natural text and within linguistic equivalence classes that preserve particular aspects of meaning or structure. Counterfactual analyses reveal selective sensitivity: changes to logical scope reduce alignment substantially more than the tested changes to hierarchical syntax, event roles, or discourse structure. Alignment also decreases when sentence structure or lexical meaning is disrupted in word lists and jabberwocky sentences, suggesting that the regularities of natural language support stronger convergence. These findings refine claims of representational universality by showing that strong overall similarity need not imply agreement in how models represent finer linguistic distinctions.

papers.title: AphaVoice: Text-to-Speech Model for Aphasia Patient Simulation
papers.abstract: While language therapy is the primary treatment for post-stroke aphasia, limited clinical resources often restrict patient access to proper care. Addressing this gap requires reliable training simulations for medical professionals. However, current AI efforts focus almost exclusively on speech processing, leaving speech generation largely unexplored. This study introduces AphaVoice, a novel text-to-speech (TTS) framework explicitly engineered to synthesize highly realistic aphasic speech. Evaluated against state-of-the-art TTS systems, AphaVoice demonstrates a superior ability to capture the clinical feature of dysfluency, outperforming existing models in temporal metrics while consistently maintaining speaker identity. By leveraging latent space shifting, the model also supports multi-speaker generation without sacrificing phonetic realism. Ultimately, AphaVoice provides a scalable, high-fidelity tool for medical training and clinical simulation related to aphasia.

papers.title: LongHisDoc: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Chinese Long Historical Document Understanding
papers.abstract: Chinese historical documents are invaluable cultural treasures, but their complexity poses significant comprehension challenges for non-specialists. Despite the success of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) in modern document tasks, their capabilities in Long (full-book) Historical Document understanding remain largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce LongHisDoc, the first benchmark tailored for long historical document understanding. LongHisDoc comprises 1,012 expert-annotated QA pairs derived from 101 PDF documents, with an average of 85.1 pages and 42,776.4 tokens per document. It spans 10 categories and features four QA types: single-page, cross-page, multi-hop, and unanswerable. Answering these questions requires integrating multimodal evidence from text, layout, and visual elements. Our evaluation reveals that the top-performing LVLM and LLM achieve only 62.9% and 69.9% accuracy, respectively, highlighting a substantial performance gap. Furthermore, we assess various modal retrievers and the end-to-end RAG performance to provide references for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. We believe that LongHisDoc serves as a comprehensive benchmark to catalyze future research in full-book historical document understanding. The benchmark and evaluation code are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/qweq12433454/LongHisDoc and https://github.com/SCUT-DLVCLab/LongHisDoc.

papers.title: Uniform Information Density-Based Preference Optimization
papers.abstract: To enable large language models to generate outputs that align with human preferences, optimization algorithms based on the comparison between chosen and rejected output pairs have been developed and been proven effective. Some recent endeavors have utilized certain linguistically-derived assumptions about the preference pairs to guide the design of more precise optimization directions. However, human preferences are complex and hard to measure by simplistic criteria, and it is important to incorporate broader and more sophisticated insights about preferred vs. not-preferred language. In this study, we adopt a well-established psycholinguistic theory, Uniform Information Density, to develop a novel preference optimization algorithm, UIDPO. The basic assumption is that humans prefer to produce language in which information is uniformly distributed, because uniformity induces less cognitive processing effort. To implement this idea into the algorithm, we derive a compound metric for information uniformity by combining the global standard deviation and the local second-order difference, and integrate it to the objective of preference optimization. We compare UIDPO with SimPO, a previous state-of-the-art method, obtaining comparable and sometimes better performance on AlpacaEval2, ArenaHard, and MT-Bench. Additional linguistic analysis on complement clauses also shows that UIDPO can better reflect the tendencies of keeping information uniform in natural language than baselines. Our results show that the subtle human preference over the information rate in language is a helpful source for achieving better human alignment for LLMs. The code repository is published here: https://github.com/CLCS-SUSTech/UIDPO.
